did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title attributes it to the descendants of Korah and identifies it as a “psalm” intended for the director of music.
Did you know? The psalm opens with thanksgiving for acts of kindness already shown: the LORD’s favor toward the land, the restoration of Jacob’s fortunes, and the forgiveness of the people’s sin.
Did you know? After describing forgiveness and reconciliation, the psalm shifts to a plea: “Restore us,” an expression asking for renewed fellowship and salvation.
Did you know? The people’s plea explicitly includes a request for life and joy: “Will you not revive us again, so that your people may rejoice in you?”
Did you know? The psalmist expects to hear a word of peace from the LORD, but adds a qualification: the people must not return to “folly,” meaning a path of foolishness or sin.
Did you know? In the psalm, salvation is described as being near those who fear the LORD, while at the same time expressing the hope that his glory will dwell in the land.

Did you know? In a particularly poetic verse, steadfast love and faithfulness are portrayed as meeting, while righteousness and peace kiss each other; this depicts a restored world in which these qualities complement one another.
Did you know? The psalm connects earth and heaven: faithfulness springs up from the earth, while righteousness looks down from heaven.
Did you know? Goodness comes from the LORD, and the land responds by yielding its harvest.
Did you know? At the conclusion, righteousness is portrayed as going before the LORD and preparing the way for his steps, giving righteousness the role of a guide and path-preparer.
